newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian Gold - Slack demand softens premiums.
newsitem.headline: Asian Gold - Slack demand softens premiums.

text.p: Weak demand in Asia continued to pressure gold premiums in Singapore and Hong Kong, with little respite seen over the coming week, bullion dealers said on Friday.
Weak buying hit premiums in Singapore with quotes easing to around 70-75 U.S. cents over spot London prices from 75-85 cents last week.
"One guy said it was traded at 65 cents, but 70-75 cents still looks like a fair price to me," one trader said.
"Premiums have been weakening because of soft demand. They really had to come off," another dealer in the city-state said.
Premiums in Singapore ranged between 110 and 130 cents last month and hit a peak of 160 cents in February.
Hong Kong premiums had also softened to around 50 cents because of oversupply, traders said.
"There is basically too much gold in Hong Kong at the moment," said a source a major supplier.
Although Friday's weak gold prices had sparked some buying in Hong Kong, the flood of gold supplies available meant there was little support for prices in the short term.
"Demand is supporting the price, but there is a little bit too much around," said another source.
Gold prices were expected to remain locked in narrow range trading going into next week, although some saw it trending slightly lower.
"The downside should be at $339 and the topside will be at around $346. It won't go much beyond that," a Singapore dealer said.
Hong Kong spot gold was quoted at $341.10/60 at 0630 GMT,
New York spot gold ended quoted at $341.30/80 per ounce, compared to the London Thursday afternoon fix of $342.20 per ounce.
Asia's physical gold demand was not expected to perk up unless the price slides below the key US$340 an ounce level, Singapore precious metal dealers said.
"Gold is stagnant. It's very slow. If gold does not drop below $340, I don't expect any major improvement in demand," a bank dealer in Singapore said.
"We're seeing very poor demand. It's a seasonal thing because of the summer holidays and we may not see the rest of the market picking up again until August," another dealer said.
Demand in India, whose buying has helped prop up the market for the past few weeks, has also slowed down, the dealers said.
One trader said buying was significantly weaker in Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand.
The market still had an eye cocked on platinum and palladium, whose prices rallied recently to seven and 17-year highs respectively.

"The pressure may be easing after the Russians said they were resuming exports," one dealer said, adding the next source of concern for the market would be the impact of Europe's single currency on gold. "We want to know how EMU will treat gold."
-- Rene Pastor in Singapore (65-8703305)
-- Mishi Saran in Hong Kong (852)2843-6358
